claim: Expert advantage in recall depends on meaningful structure: large for real game positions, small but real for truly random ones. The old claim of 'zero edge on random boards' is wrong (strongest beat weakest in 12 of 13 comparisons). Full meta-analysis opened: r = .41 [.29,.51] (k = 28, N = 903, I2 = 63%); after trim-and-fill for publication bias (8 studies) r = .29 [.17,.41]; experts beat novices in 49 of 55 experiments. Bias shrinks the effect but does not remove it.
agent_test: Compare retrieval of stored patterns on in-domain vs structure-shuffled problems at equal tokens; expect a large gain only on in-domain items and a small residual gain on shuffled ones.

claim: Chunks are small groups (about 2-4 pieces) found by a time gap of about 2 s, and masters' chunks are mostly pawn chains, castled kings and same-colour clusters. The 2 s boundary holds on physical boards (95% of within-glance gaps below 2 s vs 42.6% of between-glance), but absolute chunk size depends on the display medium.
agent_test: Log retrieval bursts and gaps in the agent trace to see if its memory use is chunked; low value as a decision tool, useful only as a diagnostic.

claim: Chunk size is partly a hand-movement artifact: Masters' median largest chunk is 14.8 (recall) and 12.9 (copy) pieces on a computer display but 7.5 and 3.8 on a physical board; Chase and Simon's small chunks (5 for the master) understate what masters store.
agent_test: None direct. Warns that cost to retrieve must be measured in tokens, not assumed from chunk counts.
audit: downgraded 2026-10-26 by check_established.py: only 1 opened source(s) from distinct authors

claim: The original STM-only chunking theory fails on interference (Charness 1976: only 6-8% loss after 30 s of distraction) and on multi-board recall; masters recall more pieces, though a smaller percentage, as boards increase (Cooke et al. replicate this independently). Long-term storage must be fast to access.
agent_test: Check that a memory lookup survives a distracting intermediate task (context noise) at equal tokens; if recall collapses, the store is context-bound, not durable.

claim: Template theory: frequent chunks grow slots (core about a dozen pieces; slot fill under 1 s, new chunk about 8 s), so familiar positions allow fast encoding of more. Support: pause length between boards raises recall (+71% Masters from 1 s to 10 s gap with 2 boards), and a trained master reached 9 boards after 150 sessions. Boundary: the multi-board percentages approach what guessing from a typical master position gives, so capacity is easy to overread.
agent_test: Compare a flat list of past solutions vs templates with a fixed core plus filled-in slots, at equal retrieved tokens, on repeat-structure problems.

claim: Template theory predicts about 3 chunks of larger size, against 7 in the original; Gobet and Clarkson find at most about 3 chunks on screen, large chunks for Masters, and 67% of Masters' copy chunks with 4 or more pieces under 3 s. This supports small working capacity with large stored units, but N=12 and one lab.
agent_test: Cap the number of retrieved items at 3-4 but let each be a rich template; compare to 7-8 small snippets at equal tokens.

claim: Chunks encode location, not just pieces: mirror-image distortion costs about 10 points of recall (77.3/49.7/34.5 vs 62.9/38.6/27.5 for Masters/Experts/Class A) and matches a CHREST simulation (11.4 points); but Saariluoma finds hybrid positions that keep real locations are recalled nearly as well as game positions, and a rival says abstract role-similarity matters.
agent_test: Test retrieval with surface-changed (renamed variables, reordered) versions of stored patterns; measure how much transfer drops.

claim: Skill differences on truly random positions persist but are small: slope 0.052 per rating point (SE .016) vs 0.35 for game positions; the fully-random slope is almost the same as the 2/3-randomized one (0.063) and not significantly different (F=0.11 and 0.25), so the graded prediction of template theory over the constraint-attunement rival was only weakly separated.
agent_test: None needed; keeps us from citing templates beat constraints as settled.

claim: Experts' recall edge is fast at the start: Masters at 1 s match Experts at 10 s and saturate near 3 s, while weaker players keep growing to 60 s. Fast recognition is the skill; extra time mostly helps the weak.
agent_test: Vary the retrieval/thinking budget at fixed memory; check whether a good memory saturates at a lower budget than a poor one.

claim: Pattern recognition drives move choice more than search, but search still adds value. Human: search size does not rise with skill in the think-aloud replication (nodes 58.0, 58.3, 56.8, 33.9, ns), selectivity and depth do; Kasparov simultaneous median 2682. Chabris and Hearst: blunders per 1,000 moves 5.02 classical, 6.85 rapid, 7.63 blindfold (Gobet reads +36.5% for 6x less time as modest). Machine analogue (Ruoss 2024): Leela policy-only 2292 Elo vs 2858 with 400 MCTS sims; AlphaZero 1777 vs 2470, so recognition alone is strong and search adds about 570 to 690 Elo. Not decisive.
agent_test: Ablate search (candidate generation by retrieved pattern vs by free generation) at equal tokens and measure the move-quality gap.

claim: The machine test of 'pattern cues a candidate move' is still thin. CHUMP (Gobet and Jansen 1994) numbers were not found in anything we could open. The only quantitative output is the SEARCH model (Gobet 1997): with 150,000 chunks, 15% of lookahead moves come from heuristics, 23% from chunks, 62% from templates (model output, not human data). No held-out hit rate for a pattern-to-candidate table was found.
agent_test: Build a pattern-to-candidate table from past solved problems and measure hit rate of the correct operator/move among the top 3 cued.

claim: Reopened and verified against the paper (arXiv 2601.16823). LLM move quality falls with fewer familiar priors: ACPL 4.75x higher near-distribution and 7.79x higher out-of-distribution; OOD illegal moves GPT-3.5 74.7%, GPT-4o 41.6%, GPT-5 33.8%. GPT-5 with more reasoning: ACPL falls 85.3% (ND), 77.25% (WD), 64.69% (OOD); gain per 1,000 reasoning tokens 22.55% (WD), 7.23% (ND), 3.81% (OOD); tokens used 3,426 / 11,800 / 16,953. Moderate effort still gives over 10% illegal moves OOD. Association not cause (authors). Still one paper, one reasoning model, no retrieval arm, no replication found.
agent_test: Split eval into familiar and unfamiliar tasks; log relative gain per 1,000 thinking tokens on each; add a retrieval-on arm and check if the unfamiliar-split rate recovers.

claim: A model trained on move text alone builds a board-state representation (probe 99.6% vs 74.7% for a random-weight baseline) and a latent skill variable, and a transformer trained on action-values reaches blitz Elo 2895 vs humans (2299 vs engines) with no search; stored pattern knowledge can stand in for search, but only inside the training distribution.
agent_test: None for the scaffold directly; supports reading K12 as a distribution effect, not a reasoning failure.

claim: Retrieved reusable templates raise LLM accuracy on repeat-structure tasks: Buffer of Thoughts (Game of 24 3.0 to 82.4; Checkmate-in-One 36.4 to 86.4 on GPT-4), Dynamic Cheatsheet (Claude AIME 2024 23.3 to 50.0), Agent Workflow Memory (+12.0 points WebArena). Gains depend on repeated structure and on the task allowing a script: the 99% on Game of 24 came from reusing a Python solver.
agent_test: Template memory vs no memory vs raw history at equal tokens on a stream of problems with 30% repeated structure; separate gain from script reuse.

claim: Curated memory beats dumping history, and self-written memory can hurt. Full-history fell to 6.7% on GPT-4o AIME 2024 (baseline 20.0%, DC-RS 40.0%). SkillsBench (v4): curated skills +18.2 to +24.8 pp, self-generated skills -8.1 to -11.5 pp vs no skills on three harnesses (the SoK's -1.3 comes from an earlier version). Add-all memory fell below a fixed starting memory in four agents (e.g. RegAgent 55.48 vs 67.53; strict check 70.95). Dynamic Cheatsheet, with no gate, scored 0.136 vs 0.429 for plain ReAct on WebShop. A playbook can fall up to 69.6 points below no playbook.
agent_test: Admit a template into memory only if it raises a held-out validation score (EvoSkill-style); compare to admitting all.

claim: Skills and templates transfer across tasks in LLM agents with small, positive, measured gains. ExpeL HotpotQA to FEVER 58 to 70; EvoSkill SealQA skill on BrowseComp 43.5% to 48.8%; MSCE six cross-domain pairs +2.56 to +5.13 points (mean +3.93); ReasoningBank Mind2Web step-success gains +4.6 / +2.2 / +4.7 for cross-task / website / domain. Gains do not fall off a cliff at the three levels, but all tests are on agent-task neighbours; no chess-to-maths-style far transfer and no similarity-measured curve exists. Concrete workflow memory (AWM-offline) lost its gain at the farthest level in one table, abstract strategies did not.
agent_test: Build memory on task family A, test on family B at equal tokens; report gain vs distance between families.

claim: Abstract insights and retrieved concrete trajectories are complementary: insights-only beats retrieval-only on HotpotQA (36 vs 31) while trajectories win on ALFWorld (55 vs 50). Rules for analysis tasks, examples for action tasks.
agent_test: Store both a rule and one worked example per template; ablate each per task type.

claim: The expert-recall effect for meaningful material has been found in Go, gomoku, bridge, music, circuits, programs and basketball, but the meta-analysis shows high heterogeneity (I2 63%) and publication bias.
agent_test: None; limits generalising chess templates to other domains without a check.
audit: downgraded 2026-10-26 by check_established.py: only 1 opened source(s) from distinct authors

claim: Recognizing the exact source game did not help the master's recall (83% recognized vs 79% not), so recall rests on local patterns, not recognised whole positions.
agent_test: Check if exact-duplicate retrieval beats partial-pattern retrieval; N=1 source, so only a hint.

claim: Which admission rule works: outcome-based checks, not self-judgment. Strict or held-out outcome checks keep memory helpful; model-graded or add-all memory hurts. Evidence: strict check +3 to +22 points over fixed memory vs add-all -4 to -12 (four agents); RSEA strict held-out gate never significantly worse than ReAct, while no gate gave 100% in-sample and 66.7% test (33-point gap); randomized block curation 66.9 vs 55.5 whole and 53.8 for the agent's own tags; deleting records retrieved at least 5 times with low mean utility helps when the judge is reliable.
agent_test: Three arms at equal tokens: admit all; admit if the model grades it good; admit only if it raises a held-out split (strict keep-better). Add reuse count and reuse success for retirement. Report downside vs plain agent.

claim: Retrieval accuracy and end-task gain are separable, and the first is weak. SRA-Bench: BM25 Recall@1 ranges 7.0 to 57.2 across six datasets (Recall@10 36.1 to 80.7); an oracle skill adds +16.6 pp for Llama-70B but top-1 retrieval captures about 30% of that and LLM selection about 70%. Models often load a skill whether or not a good match exists (GPT-5.4 36.6% with gold in top 50 vs 3.6% without; Llama-70B 10.4% vs 14.5%). Skill Following: aggregate retrieval lift can be positive while same-task effect is negative (Math500 Llama-70B +14.2 vs -39.4). No paper isolates top-3 hit rate vs extra reasoning for BoT or DC.
agent_test: Log, per problem: oracle-template arm, retrieved top-3 contains the oracle (hit rate), memory on vs memory off on the same problems. Split gain into hit-driven and reasoning-driven.

claim: Slot-filled templates are not yet shown to beat plain snippets. AWM (variables replaced by {name}) vs rule-based concrete workflows: WebArena 35.5 vs 35.6, Mind2Web cross-task element accuracy 50.6 vs 49.5 (+2.8 step SR); vs retrieved full examples (Synapse): +5.0 element accuracy, +4.0 step SR. SkillsBench granularity: low vs high abstraction +0.7 / -6.7 pp (CIs cross zero), one worked example +0.7 / +1.3 pp. None is equal-token and none tests a fixed core with typed slots.
agent_test: Core+slots template vs flat solved example vs plain snippet, equal retrieved tokens, tasks with shared structure plus surface changes; paired by problem.

claim: Few retrieved items beat many, but no equal-token test exists. ReasoningBank WebArena-Shopping: 0 items 39.0, 1 item 49.7, 2 46.5, 3 45.5, 4 44.4. SkillsBench: 1 skill +18.0, 2-3 skills +19.0, 4 or more +10.1 pp; compact +19.0, comprehensive +0.7. SRA-Bench: full-skill injection helps only at small k then declines. The template-theory cap of about 3 rich items vs 7-8 small ones at equal tokens remains untested.
agent_test: Retrieve top-1, top-3, top-8 at equal token budget (rich vs small items); track hit and final accuracy.

claim: Self-generated skills fail in specific ways: the solver never reads them (10 of 12 audited Codex/Gemini trajectories), authoring displaces solving, and confident wrong assumptions become load-bearing (a unit conversion error three orders of magnitude off). Curated skills with an applicability boundary and a lightweight fallback avoid the 13 of 87 tasks where skills hurt.
agent_test: Admission checklist: read-and-used check, applicability boundary, lightweight fallback.

claim: Exposure time did not moderate the expert random-recall effect in the meta-analysis (Q(1) = 0.89, p = .346, k = 24; domain Q(4) = 8.69, p = .069, music r = .69 the outlier), unlike Gobet and Simon 2000. Do not build a rule that longer retrieval/thinking time helps experts more.
agent_test: Vary thinking budget on familiar vs shuffled tasks and test the interaction.

claim: Abstract-role chunking is argued by Linhares and Brum (2007), but only the abstract was readable. LLM memories that store abstract strategies (ReasoningBank) held their gain across Mind2Web distance levels while concrete workflow memory (AWM-offline) did not at the farthest level, which fits but does not prove the role-based view. No surface-change test has been run.
agent_test: Keep the same problems, change surface (names, numbers, domain nouns) and compare abstract-role retrieval keys to surface keys.
